parts.title: How two switches control the gate

orientation.place: This is the only part of the sample. It shows every stage of the new study cycle on a tiny synthetic source.
orientation.purpose: You will be able to state the gate rule, predict the gate for any switch setting and explain why the display can mislead.
orientation.prereq: No background is needed; everything comes from source S1.

summary.md: This part covers how two switches control a fictional **gate**. The gate is open only when **switch A** and **switch B** are both on. If either switch is off, the gate stays **closed**. A **sensor** displays the gate state, but a broken sensor can show **OPEN** while the gate is closed. You will distinguish the rule about the gate from what its display shows.

keywords.definition: The fictional Luma gate whose state depends on two switches.
The two switches; both must be on for the gate to open.
The gate state whenever at least one switch is off.
Displays the gate state; it can be broken.
What the display may show even when the gate is closed.

kazanimlar.title: The gate rule
kazanimlar.objective: Without notes, state when the gate is open and predict it for any switch setting.

blocks.md: In the Luma system the gate is **open if and only if both switches A and B are on** (S1 ¶1). "If and only if" means two things at once: both on → open, and open → both on.
One switch on is never enough: the rule needs **both** (S1 ¶1).

practice.stem: Embedded check (not counted): with A on and B on, what does the rule say?
practice.solution: Both switches are on, so the gate is open (S1 ¶1).

recall.prompt: Without notes: when is the Luma gate open, and what happens if one switch is off?
recall.model_answer: It is open only if both switches A and B are on; if either switch is off, it stays closed.
key_points: both A and B on → open

priming.summary_md: The **gate** has one rule: it is open only when **switch A** and **switch B** are both on. Any setting with a switch off leaves it **closed**.

keywords.definition: The two switches; both must be on for the gate to open.

priming.purpose: State the gate rule and predict the gate for any switch setting.

feynman.prompt: Explain the gate rule to a classmate: when is the gate open, and what happens for each of the four switch settings?

kazanimlar.title: Display versus actual state
kazanimlar.objective: Without notes, explain why OPEN on the display does not prove that the gate is open.

blocks.md: The sensor only **displays** the state. S1 adds that a **broken sensor can display OPEN even while the gate is closed** (S1 ¶1). So the display is an observation that can be wrong; the switch rule decides the actual state.
Do not read the display as the rule: OPEN on the screen is not evidence that A and B are both on.

recall.prompt: Without notes: why can't you conclude that the gate is open just because the display shows OPEN?
recall.model_answer: Because a broken sensor can display OPEN while the gate is actually closed.
key_points: the display alone is not enough
a broken sensor can show OPEN while closed

priming.summary_md: A **sensor** shows the gate state on a display. The display can be wrong: a broken sensor can show **OPEN** while the gate is closed.

priming.purpose: Explain why OPEN on the display does not by itself show that the gate is open.

items.stem: *S1, exercise 1.* A is on and B is off. Is the gate open or closed? Say why.

criteria.text: Gives the reason: both switches must be on.

rubric.model: Closed: the gate opens only when both A and B are on, and B is off (S1 ¶1; supplied key: closed).

hints: Look at what the rule needs from **both** switches.

steps.why: The rule also needs B on, so the condition fails.

items.solution: Closed. B is off, and the gate is open only when both switches are on (S1 ¶1).

items.stem: A is off and B is on. What is the gate state?

option_notes.c: The rule, not the display, decides the state (S1 ¶1).

hints: Is there any setting with one switch off that opens the gate?
items.solution: Closed: either switch off keeps the gate closed (S1 ¶1).

option_notes.a: Both on is the only setting that opens the gate.

items.stem: State the condition under which the Luma gate is open.

criteria.text: Both A and B must be on (and only then).

items.stem: Switch A is on, switch B is off, and the display shows OPEN. Which statements are true?

options.md: The display proves the gate is open.
The display is right, so the switch rule does not apply here.

option_notes.a: Correct: B is off, so the rule keeps the gate closed (S1 ¶1).
option_notes.b: The display alone is not enough; a broken sensor can show OPEN while the gate is closed (S1 ¶1).
option_notes.c: Correct: a broken sensor can show OPEN while the gate is closed (S1 ¶1).
option_notes.d: The rule always decides the gate; the display can be wrong (S1 ¶1).

items.solution: B is off, so the gate is closed (the rule needs both switches on). The display then shows OPEN while the gate is closed, which a broken sensor can do (S1 ¶1). True: a and c.

blocks.title: Connect the two topics
items: The switches decide the gate: open only when A and B are both on (S1 ¶1).
The display only reports the state and can be wrong: a broken sensor can show OPEN while the gate is closed (S1 ¶1).
When the switches and the display disagree, the switch rule decides.

criteria.text: Both switches A and B are on (and only then).

rubric.model: Both A and B must be on; that is the only setting in which it is open (S1 ¶1).

final_test.stem: Switch A is off, switch B is on, and the display shows OPEN. According to the rule, what is the actual gate state?

final_test.solution: It closes: B off breaks the both-switches condition (S1 ¶1).
